latin.288: Certe Chamierus negavit actionem illam Adami esse nostram actionem, lib. 1. de hom. corrupt. c. 8. § 9. Dico, inquit, nullum peccatum unum numero posse esse commune omnibus hominibus. Nam peccatum, vel qualitas est, vel actio. Qualitas, ut peccatum originale. Actio, ut peccatum quodlibet actuale. At nulla qualitas, una eademque numero potest pluribus subjectis communicari: ut candor qui est in nive, idem numero non potest esse in cygno, aut lana. Actiones autem sunt suppositorum. Quare idem homicidium a Caino patratum non potest esse a Lamecho. Itaque nego peccatum illud Adami esse peccatum Originale. Non enim potest omnibus esse commune, sive numero, quia est actio: sive specie, quia est individuus actus. Et rursus eodem capite § 11. Omne peccatum vel qualitas est, vel actio, ut diximus, eius cujus dicitur peccatum. At hic actus Adami, neque qualitas est nostra: nam ne est quidem: ac proinde non potest esse qualitas: tum actio, qualitasque longe differunt: neque est etiam actus noster: quia idem numero actus non est variorum suppositorum. Ergo is actus Adami non est nostrum peccatum: nedum sit nostrum originale. Haec eius ratio eadem est cum hac mea, si actio Adami est nostra, eius suppositum est nostrum: Sunt enim actiones suppositorum.
latin.289: Justitia enim non modo non exigit, sed ne patitur quidem, ut judiciaria imputatione peccatum fiat eius peccatum, cujus alioqui peccatum non fuisset. Faceret enim peccatorem judex, alioqui non peccatorem, id quod cum judicis officio pugnat, ut quod maxime. Itaque frustra observat vir doctus alienas personas non imputari, sed actiones. Non enim sic argumentabar; si actio Adami nobis imputatur, etiam nobis imputatur eius persona: Sed contendebam nullam reddi posse causam idoneam, cur illa actio nobis imputetur immediate; ac inter caeteras hanc excludebam, nostram esse actionem illam Adami: ac proinde nobis jure imputari. Intelligebatur igitur esse nostra, non per imputationem immediatam, sed ante illam: quo modo dici non potest, cur magis nostra sit, quam ipsa persona Adami. Non igitur id quod dixi vir doctus oppugnat, sed aliud quid.
latin.290: Interim quaero dum alia peccata committeret (commisisse enim haud dubie non negabis) an non fuerit etiam tum primus homo, origo, stirps, seu radix omnium hominum? Fuisse proculdubio concedas: fueruntne igitur ea quoque eodem modo considerata, & justo Dei judicio omnibus hominibus imputata? Si negas, fatearis oportet hujus considerationis judicii & imputationis primi peccati, quam protulisti in medium, rationem hanc non esse, quia Adam primus homo fuit, & origo, & stirps omnium hominum. Si affirmas, Revincet te Apostolus Rom. v. tam unitatem peccati quam hominis unitatem inculcans. Quaererem etiam libenter de Setho, de Noacho, aliisque ejusmodi stirpibus totius, quod extat, generis humani, num eorum quoque peccata eodem modo fuerint & considerata, & imputata posteris? Si fuerunt, multos homines dicere debuit Apostolus Rom. v. non unum, &, nos antequam nascamur miserrimi, qui tot peccata commisimus. Si non fuerunt, discriminis peto rationem: sed vereor ne sim longior hoc loco quam necesse est.
latin.291: GAR. Quod vero docent Theologi Adamum peccasse ut caput hominum, & jure posteris imputari primam illam eius inobedientiam, variis quaestionum & erotematum machinis quatit, quibus & alii nonnulla etiam addunt, quae omnia hic in unum fasciculum compingemus. PLAC. Nec Adamo elogium capitis hominum detraho, nec jure posteris imputari primam illam eius inobedientiam nego, si imputari intelligatur mediante corruptione ex ipsa in nos propagata. Tantum nego ita Adamum ut caput hominum peccasse, ut nobis possit, aut debeat prima eius inobedientia imputari immediate. Sunt autem hae quaestiones partim e Thesibus meis, partim ex hoc posteriore Manuscripto omnes, praeter unam, excerptae. Itaque non omnes sunt hujus loci; non erit tamen inutile eas hoc loco a responsionibus viri docti tutas praestare: quoniam in illis de causa agitur, ob quam peccatum illud immediate dicitur imputari; cui investigandae hoc caput destinatum est.
latin.292: GAR. 1. Si peccavit ut caput generis humani, cur non etiam puniri debuit eo nomine? 2. Cur potius Adami peccatum posteris, quam posterorum Adae imputatur? 3. Cum Adamus post illud peccatum, confestim non desierit esse caput, cur non sequentia Adami peccata aeque posteris imputantur atque primum? 4. Cur potius actuale peccatum, quod est actio transiens, imputari dicitur, quam habituale, quod fuit vitium permanens? 5. Si primus actus peccandi fuit actus naturae, cur non etiam primus actus generandi? Nemo tamen dixerit nos in Adamo Cainum aut Sethum genuisse. 6. Si ut Christi justitia nobis imputatur, ita & peccatum Adae nostrum est imputatione, cur non, ut Christus dicitur, justitia nostra, dicitur etiam Adamus peccatum nostrum? 7. Cum dicimur peccasse in Adamo, estne propria, an impropria locutio? Propria dici non potest, nisi dicamus, aliquid simul esse & non esse: proprie enim loquendo, tum cum Adamus peccavit, fuissemus, non fuissemus. Si propria non est, revocanda est ad propriam. Quid autem significat proprie nos fuisse in Adamo, nisi nos ducere ab Adamo originem, vel esse Adami esse causam nostri esse?
latin.293: GAR. VII. Nos vero respondemus. I. Generaliter. Si ejusmodi interrogationum punctulis locus esse debeat, non minus speciose sollicitari posse doctrinam de corruptione Originali a Pelagii aut Socini sectatoribus, quam haec de imputatione doctrina hic vexatur. Quaeretur enim 1. Cur Adami corruptio moralis posteros potius infecit, quam corruptio posterorum inquinavit Adamum? 2. Cur Adami peccatum in posteros necessario descendit, caeterorum patrum non ita descendit? 3. Cur Adami peccatum Caino nocuit, Caini peccatum Adamo minime nocuit? 4. Cur primum peccatum nos potius corrupit, quam sequentia? 5. Cur Adamus ab illa corruptione liberatus est ... infantes omnes ... non liberantur? 6. Cur Christus justitia & sanctificatio nostra dicitur, Adamus non dicitur peccatum & corruptio nostra? Haec & alia adversus doctrinam de corruptione ingenita queri possunt, quae si non obstant quominus Viri docti corruptionem illam agnoscere debeant; neque debent quaestiunculae illae impedimento nobis esse, quominus in antiqua & Catholica imputationis fide perseveremus. PLAC. Itane antiqua & catholica est imputationis immediatae fides? Id neque probatum est hactenus, neque probari potest.

pass_a.288: Chamier flatly denies that Adam's act is our act (On human corruption 1.8 §§9, 11). No one numerically identical sin can be common to all: sin is quality or act—original as quality, actual as act. One numerical quality cannot belong to many subjects (snow's whiteness is not the swan's or wool's). Acts belong to individuals (supposits): Cain's murder is not Lamech's. So Adam's sin is not original sin—not common by number (it is an act) nor by species (it is an individual act). That act is neither our quality (it does not even exist as ours) nor our act (the same numerical act is not of various subjects). Hence it is not our sin, still less our original. His ground matches mine: if Adam's act is ours, his subject is ours—for acts are of subjects.
pass_a.289: Justice does not demand—and will not allow—that by judicial imputation a sin become his who otherwise had no sin: that would have the judge make a non-sinner into a sinner, against the judge's office. So the learned man wastes effort noting that alien persons are not imputed, only actions. I never argued: if Adam's act is imputed to us, his person is too. I argued no fit cause appears why that act is immediately imputed to us, and among other candidates I ruled out 'because it is our act' as the ground of right imputation. 'Ours' was meant before immediate imputation, not by it—and then one cannot say why it is more ours than Adam's person. He fights something other than what I said.
pass_a.290: Meanwhile, while he committed other sins (you will hardly deny he did), was he not still first man, origin, stock, root of all? You will grant he was. Were those later sins likewise considered and by God's just judgment imputed to all? If you deny, you must admit the reason you floated for considering/judging/imputing the first sin is not 'because Adam was first man and origin of all.' If you affirm, the Apostle in Romans 5, pressing both the unity of the sin and the unity of the man, refutes you. I would also ask about Seth, Noah, and like stocks of the surviving race: were their sins so considered and imputed to posterity? If yes, Romans 5 should have said many men, not one, and we are wretched before birth for so many sins. If no, give the distinction—though I fear I run long here.
pass_a.291: GAR: What theologians teach—that Adam sinned as head of men and that first disobedience is rightly imputed to posterity—he shakes with assorted questions and erotemata, with others' additions, which we here bind in one bundle. PLAC: I neither strip Adam of the title 'head of men' nor deny that first disobedience is rightly imputed to posterity if that means by means of the corruption propagated from it into us. I only deny that he sinned as head so that his first disobedience can or ought to be imputed to us immediately. These questions are drawn partly from my Theses, partly from this later Manuscript—all but one. Not all belong here; still it helps to secure them against the learned man's replies, since they treat the cause for which that sin is said to be immediately imputed—the very inquiry this chapter is for.
pass_a.292: GAR's seven: (1) If he sinned as head of the race, why not also be punished under that title? (2) Why is Adam's sin imputed to posterity rather than posterity's to Adam? (3) Since he did not at once cease to be head after that sin, why are later sins not equally imputed? (4) Why impute the actual (a passing act) rather than the habitual (a lasting vice)? (5) If the first act of sinning was an act of nature, why not the first act of begetting—yet no one says we in Adam begot Cain or Seth? (6) If Adam's sin is ours by imputation as Christ's righteousness is, why is Christ called our righteousness but Adam not called our sin? (7) Is 'we sinned in Adam' proper or improper speech? Proper speech cannot say we both were and were not when Adam sinned; if improper, reduce it—and properly, being in Adam means drawing origin from him, or his being as remote cause of ours.
pass_a.293: GAR answers generally: if such pinpoint questions are allowed, Pelagians or Socinians could as speciously harry original corruption as this imputation doctrine is harried here—why Adam's moral corruption infected posterity rather than theirs him; why his sin must descend and other fathers' not; why his hurt Cain but Cain's not him; why the first corrupted us more than later ones; why Adam was freed and infants not; why Christ is our righteousness/sanctification but Adam not our sin/corruption. If those do not block acknowledging inborn corruption, neither should these quibbles stop perseverance in the old Catholic faith of imputation. PLAC: Is immediate imputation's faith thus ancient and catholic? That is neither proved yet nor proveable.

288: Certainly Chamier denied that that action of Adam is our action, book 1 On the corruption of man, chapter 8, § 9. I say, he says, that no sin one in number can be common to all men. For sin is either a quality or an action. A quality, as original sin. An action, as any actual sin whatever. But no quality, one and the same in number, can be communicated to several subjects: as the whiteness which is in snow cannot be the same in number in a swan, or in wool. But actions are of individuals (supposits). Therefore the same homicide perpetrated by Cain cannot be by Lamech. Therefore I deny that that sin of Adam is Original sin. For it cannot be common to all, whether by number, because it is an action: or by species, because it is an individual act. And again in the same chapter § 11. Every sin is either a quality or an action, as we have said, of him of whom it is called a sin. But this act of Adam is neither a quality of ours: for it does not even exist: and therefore it cannot be a quality: then action and quality differ widely: nor is it even our act: because the same act in number is not of various subjects. Therefore that act of Adam is not our sin: much less is it our original. This reason of his is the same as this of mine: if Adam's action is ours, his subject is ours: for actions are of subjects.
289: For justice not only does not require, but does not even suffer, that by judicial imputation a sin should become the sin of him whose sin it would otherwise not have been. For the judge would make a sinner of one otherwise not a sinner—which conflicts with the judge's office as much as anything can. Therefore the learned man observes in vain that alien persons are not imputed, but actions. For I was not arguing thus: if Adam's action is imputed to us, his person also is imputed to us. But I was contending that no fit cause can be given why that action should be imputed to us immediately; and among the rest I was excluding this—that that action of Adam is ours, and therefore is justly imputed to us. It was understood, then, to be ours not through immediate imputation, but before it: in which way it cannot be said why it is more ours than Adam's person itself. Therefore it is not what I said that the learned man attacks, but something else.
290: Meanwhile I ask: while he was committing other sins (for you will scarcely deny that he committed them), was he not even then the first man, the origin, stock, or root of all men? That he was, you will doubtless grant: were those also, then, considered in the same way, and by God's just judgment imputed to all men? If you deny, you must confess that this reason of the consideration, judgment, and imputation of the first sin which you brought forward is not this—because Adam was the first man, and the origin and stock of all men. If you affirm, the Apostle in Romans 5 will refute you, inculcating the unity of the sin as much as the unity of the man. I would also gladly ask about Seth, about Noah, and other such stocks of the whole human race that remains, whether their sins also were in the same way both considered and imputed to posterity. If they were, the Apostle in Romans 5 ought to have said many men, not one, and we, before we are born, are most wretched, who have committed so many sins. If they were not, I ask the reason of the distinction: but I fear I may be longer in this place than is necessary.
291: GAR. But what the theologians teach—that Adam sinned as the head of men, and that that first disobedience of his is rightly imputed to posterity—he shakes with various engines of questions and erotemata, to which others also add some things, all of which we will here bind into one fascicle. PLAC. Neither do I strip Adam of the title of head of men, nor do I deny that that first disobedience of his is rightly imputed to posterity, if it is understood to be imputed by means of the corruption propagated from it into us. I only deny that Adam so sinned as the head of men that his first disobedience can or ought to be imputed to us immediately. Now these questions are all excerpted partly from my Theses, partly from this later Manuscript, except one. Therefore not all are of this place; yet it will not be useless to keep them safe in this place from the learned man's replies: since in them the debate is about the cause on account of which that sin is said to be immediately imputed—to the investigating of which this chapter is destined.
292: GAR. 1. If he sinned as the head of the human race, why ought he not also to have been punished under that title? 2. Why is Adam's sin rather imputed to posterity than posterity's to Adam? 3. Since Adam after that sin did not at once cease to be head, why are Adam's following sins not equally imputed to posterity as the first? 4. Why is actual sin, which is a transient action, rather said to be imputed than habitual, which was a permanent vice? 5. If the first act of sinning was an act of nature, why not also the first act of begetting? Yet no one would say that we in Adam begot Cain or Seth. 6. If as Christ's righteousness is imputed to us, so also Adam's sin is ours by imputation, why is Christ called our righteousness, but Adam is not also called our sin? 7. When we are said to have sinned in Adam, is it proper or improper speech? It cannot be called proper unless we say that something simultaneously is and is not: for properly speaking, when Adam sinned, we would have been, we would not have been. If it is not proper, it must be reduced to the proper. But what does it properly signify that we were in Adam, except that we draw origin from Adam, or that Adam's being is the cause of our being?
293: GAR. VII. But we answer. I. Generally. If there ought to be room for such pinpoint interrogations, the doctrine of Original corruption can be no less speciously harassed by the followers of Pelagius or Socinus than this doctrine of imputation is vexed here. For it would be asked 1. Why Adam's moral corruption rather infected posterity than posterity's corruption stained Adam? 2. Why Adam's sin necessarily descended into posterity, and that of other fathers not so? 3. Why Adam's sin hurt Cain, and Cain's sin hurt Adam not at all? 4. Why the first sin rather corrupted us than Adam's following sins? 5. Why was Adam freed from that corruption ... and all infants ... not freed? 6. Why is Christ called our righteousness and sanctification, and Adam not called our sin and corruption? These and other things can be asked against the doctrine of inborn corruption, which if they do not hinder the learned man from having to acknowledge that corruption, neither ought those little questions to be an impediment to us from persevering in the ancient and Catholic faith of imputation. PLAC. Is the faith of immediate imputation thus ancient and catholic? That has neither been proved thus far, nor can it be proved.
